requirement: GitHub Actions MUST run `cargo test --locked --workspace` and `mdbook test` for pull requests and pushes to `main`. After those checks pass on `main`, it MUST build the book and deploy the generated `book/` directory to GitHub Pages. The book MUST set `output.html.site-url` to `/habeas-codicem/` for project-site hosting.
rationale:
**Judgment: false.** The workflow does what the requirement says, but nothing is marked as implementing it.

**What the workflow does**
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` triggers on `push` to `main` and on `pull_request`.
- The `test-and-build` job runs `cargo test --locked --workspace` and `mdbook test`, then `mdbook build`.
- The `deploy` job runs only for a push to `refs/heads/main` and needs `test-and-build`. It calls `actions/deploy-pages@v4`, and `test-and-build` uploads the `book` directory as the Pages artifact.
- `book.toml:13` sets `site-url = "/habeas-codicem/"`.

**Gaps**
1. **No `{impl}` markers.** The `references` lookup for `requirements.integration.ci` returns no sites. A repo-wide search finds no `{impl}`, `{test}` or `{cite}` reference to it in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` or `book.toml`.
   - The project already marks non-Rust files this way, for example `book.toml:6` for `requirements.cli.mdbook` and `Cargo.toml:13` for the symposium requirements.
   - The workflow's test, build and deploy steps and the `site-url` setting therefore implement the requirement without being marked. Under the review criteria, that is a gap.
2. **Unspecified behavior in the workflow.** `ci.yml` also does things the requirement does not state, and no other definition covers them:
   - It sets up Node 24 and runs `node --test .github/scripts/autofix.test.mjs`.
   - It installs mdBook 0.5.4 with `cargo install`.
   - It runs a separate `symposium-hook` job, which installs symposium 0.5.1 and runs `tests/symposium_hook_smoke.py`.
   - The deploy job also waits on that `symposium-hook` job.
   - It uses `configure-pages` and `upload-pages-artifact` steps.

   Most of this is plausibly supporting infrastructure, but none of it is tied to a requirement.
3. **No tests, and no stated justification.** No `{test}` reference exists. A CI workflow is hard to unit test, so the absence could be justified, but nothing in the sources says so. Checks that `ci.yml` has the right commands, triggers and `site-url` could be written, but none exist.

Adding `{impl}` comments in `ci.yml` and `book.toml`, covering the extra jobs with a requirement or marking them, and recording why the workflow has no tests would close these gaps. No FIXME acknowledges any of them.

Calling code that implements a definition does not count. An example must reference a requirement with `{test}` or `{cite}`, so an example reference still traces the function to a requirement. Run `habeas author --all` to create requirement and example evidence. Each assessment has its own model conversation. Each requirement's review receives the sources marked `{impl}` or `{test}` for it and can look up every source that references it, so it can find implementing code that is unmarked or only cited. It records delivered source inputs and writes judgments and rationales. The supervising agent must not compose or refresh evidence JSON, determinations, rationales, or snapshots itself, or delegate manual evidence writing to another agent. If authoring configuration or credentials are unavailable, report the blocker instead of substituting hand-written evidence.

The authoring harness assesses whether the code marked `{impl}` for a requirement implements every obligation completely and exactly as stated, and whether tests cover interesting design cases. It also treats as gaps any code that implements part of the requirement without `{impl}`, including code that only cites it, and any behavior in `{impl}` code that no definition implemented there specifies. When another requirement implements part of the subject, it checks only that the text carries out that part. For absent tests, it assesses whether simplicity or impracticality justifies their absence. For an example, it assesses whether test setup and assertions cover the scenario and expected outcomes. Use these criteria while implementing and fixing reported gaps; leave evidence judgments and rationales to the harness.

Inspect every end-user-observable result and branch, including errors and input handling. Check that the code fulfills each applicable requirement and introduces no additional observable behavior without an agreed requirement. When requirements interact, mark every requirement implemented at the relevant point with `{impl}` and explain how their texts jointly account for the behavior. A reference alone does not explain why a behavior, such as accepting `^C`, is specified.

Every explicit function or method in first-party Rust sources needs its own requirement or example reference in an attached Rust comment or within its body, including trait methods and test helpers. A reference on an enclosing module or `impl` does not cover its functions, and there is no uncited-function waiver. If no existing requirement explains an internal helper, propose a requirement scoped to that area of internal code, such as `internal.config_parsing`, rather than one catch-all, get the user's agreement, and mark the helper with `{impl}`. That requirement's review checks that it explains each implementing function. Do not use an internal-detail requirement to justify otherwise unspecified observable behavior.

Write a concrete case as a separate `{example}` directive with the same chapter-qualified naming and fence rules. Reference at least one requirement it illustrates from the example body: `{test}` when the example is a case the requirement's review should check, `{cite}` when the requirement is context for the example's own review, or both. A true example determination needs test references and an evidence rationale explaining how the tests cover its interesting aspects. Keep names unique across requirements and examples.

- `{impl}`: it implements part of the definition, making a decision, performing a check, producing an output, or handling a case the definition specifies. Calling code that implements the definition, or producing a result a caller uses to meet it, does not count. A requirement that refines another's obligation can `{impl}` it. A convention for every output of a kind, such as every validation error, is implemented by the code that carries it out as a whole.
- `{test}`: it is designed to verify behavior the definition specifies, through a test's scenario and assertions or an example's concrete case. Incidental setup does not count.
- `{cite}`: it relies on, supports, or refers to the definition without implementing or testing it.

`{impl}` and `{test}` make the source an input to the definition's assessment and must be covered by its evidence. `{cite}` makes the cited definition context for the citing requirement or example, needs no coverage, and does not count toward the cited requirement's implementation.

Rust-item selectors use syntactic ancestry within one repository-relative file. Examples include `mod[local]/fn[run]`, `impl[Thing]/fn[run]`, `impl[Thing/Trait]/fn[run]`, `trait[Trait]/fn[read]`, `fn[outer]/fn[inner]`, and positional `use#1`. Duplicate sibling names gain `#1`, `#2`, and so on. Delimiter characters and whitespace within names or impl types use percent-encoded UTF-8 bytes, so spelling can be recovered without resolving modules across files. {cite}`requirements.references.rust_item_selectors`

Habeas's bundled agent skills MUST direct agents reviewing code against requirements to inspect every end-user-observable result and branch, including errors and input handling, and verify both that the code fulfills each applicable requirement and that it introduces no additional end-user-observable behavior without an agreed requirement. They MUST explain the requirement and example review criteria in {cite}`requirements.ci.review_criteria`, including test adequacy and justified absence of tests for requirements, and the three outcomes and documented-gap convention in {cite}`requirements.ci.outcomes`. Agents MUST mark code that implements part of a requirement with `{impl}` and tests that verify it with `{test}`, using `{cite}` only for related code that does neither, under {cite}`requirements.references.targets`. Where requirements interact, agents MUST mark every requirement implemented at the relevant point and explain how their texts jointly account for the behavior. A citation alone MUST NOT count as that explanation.

Habeas's bundled agent skills MUST NOT offer a waiver for an uncited first-party Rust function. When a function serves only as an internal implementation detail and no existing requirement explains it, Habeas's bundled agent skills MUST direct agents to propose an explicit project requirement scoped to one area of internal code, such as `internal.config_parsing`, rather than one catch-all requirement, obtain the user's agreement, mark the function with `{impl}`, and run `habeas author --all` for the harness to assess that requirement's evidence. That assessment MUST account for whether the requirement explains each implementing function's behavior. An internal-detail requirement MUST NOT justify an otherwise unspecified end-user-observable behavior.

An mdBook chapter MAY define an example with an opening fence of at least three colons immediately followed by `{example} <name>` and a closing colon-only fence of at least the opening length. The full name MUST use the same chapter-derived namespace and valid-name rules as `{req}`. The body MUST include all Markdown between the fences, excluding surrounding whitespace, and MUST describe a concrete case with expected behavior. An example MUST contain at least one valid `{cite}` or `{test}` reference to a requirement it illustrates; `{cite}` makes the requirement an input to the example's assessment, and `{test}` makes the example an input to the requirement's assessment, under {cite}`requirements.references.targets`. An example MAY use both. An example directive inside a fenced code block MUST remain literal.

Every defined example MUST have an `evidence/<full-example-name>.json` file whose `example` string exactly matches the current example body. A true determination MUST have at least one `{test}` reference to the example, covered by an evidence input. The reviewer MUST assess its tests under {cite}`requirements.ci.review_criteria` and use the outcomes defined by {cite}`requirements.ci.outcomes`; the no-test justification for a requirement MUST NOT establish a true example judgment. Habeas MUST apply the same missing-evidence, determination, input validation, and reference-coverage checks used for requirements. It MUST report a true determination with no test reference and changed example text with a compact line-oriented diff.

When a `{requirements-index}` chapter exists, it MUST list examples as well as requirements, identify each entry's kind, and show each example's evidence state. Example detail pages and their links MUST follow {cite}`requirements.index.detail_pages` and {cite}`requirements.index.navigation`; references to an example MUST link to its definition.

An mdBook chapter MAY contain one standalone `{requirements-index}` directive with an empty body, opened by at least three colons and closed by at least as many. A book MUST contain no more than one such directive. When present, `habeas mdbook` MUST replace it with a table of all requirements defined in rendered chapters, each linking to its evidence detail page under {cite}`requirements.index.detail_pages`.

Each evidence detail page MUST display its state as a Shields.io static badge image with meaningful alt text and the current requirement or example body as a Markdown block quote labeled by kind. It MUST render the recorded rationale as Markdown in a Rationale section and display the recorded FIXME strings when the determination is FIXME. Inputs MUST be grouped under headings in this order: Implementation, for sources reached by an `{impl}` edge from the definition, including anchored files; Tests, for sources reached by a `{test}` edge, including tests, examples, and anchored files; Referenced definitions, for declarations the definition cites and their terminology; and Other sources, for the remaining inputs the assessment consulted. Edges MUST be determined from the current references under {cite}`requirements.references.targets` and {cite}`requirements.references.anchors`. Each group and each input MUST be a collapsible disclosure element, with groups expanded and inputs collapsed by default, so readers can move between groups and open individual sources. Each input MUST have its own subsection identifying its selector. A file-range or Rust-item input MUST show its resolved file and inclusive line range. A requirements input MUST show its selection and each matched definition's full name, file, and inclusive line range. Each subsection MUST show the exact recorded text in a fenced code block. Code fences MUST request Rust highlighting for `.rs` files and language-aware highlighting for Markdown, JSON, TOML, Java, JavaScript, TypeScript, and Python files; TOML MAY use INI highlighting when native TOML highlighting is unavailable.

Project text files MAY use the `{impl}`, `{cite}`, and `{test}` roles with a backtick-delimited full requirement or example name. Each reference is a directed edge between its source and the named definition. A source is a project source item or a requirement or example declaration. `{cite}` MUST mean that the source relies on, supports, or refers to the definition, and is an edge from the source to the definition. `{impl}` MUST mean that the source implements part of the definition: it makes a decision, performs a check, produces an output, or handles a case that the definition specifies. A requirement MAY implement part of another requirement by refining one of its obligations. Calling code that implements a definition, or producing a result a caller uses to meet it, MUST NOT by itself count as implementing it. A requirement stating a convention for every output of a kind, such as every validation error, is implemented by the source that carries out the convention as a whole, such as the step that collects and reports those outputs. `{test}` MUST mean that the source is designed to verify behavior the definition specifies: a test through its scenario and the assertions about that scenario's outcome, or a named example through the concrete case it describes. `{impl}` and `{test}` are edges from the definition to the source. Only requirements and examples are assessed; code is reviewed as part of the definitions it implements or tests. During repository validation, Habeas MUST parse every first-party Rust source file in the project. Every explicitly declared function or method, including trait methods and test helpers, and every struct, enum, and union MUST have a valid `{impl}`, `{cite}`, or `{test}` reference to a defined requirement or named example in a Rust comment attached to it or within its body. A comment immediately preceding an item's declaration or its attributes is attached to that item. A comment within an item's body, including one before a field, variant, or attribute inside it, belongs to the smallest enclosing item. A named example MUST reference a requirement under {cite}`requirements.examples.definition`. A reference in a string literal, on an enclosing module or impl block, or only in an evidence input MUST NOT count for the items it encloses. Habeas MUST report every unreferenced item with its file, line, kind, and name, and MUST report a Rust parse failure instead of silently skipping the file.

Habeas MUST identify a Rust item by the pair of its `rust_file`, following the path rules in {cite}`requirements.ci.schema`, and a `rust_item` selector derived from a `syn` parse of that file. The selector MUST describe syntactic ancestry within the file and MUST NOT resolve Rust modules across files or use line numbers as identity. Named items MUST use kind-and-name segments such as `fn[run]` and `struct[Packet]`. Impl segments MUST distinguish inherent from trait impls using their syntactic self type and optional trait path. Otherwise identical selectors MUST have deterministic source-order disambiguators. A `use` declaration MUST have a positional selector `use#N`, where N is its one-based position among sibling `use` declarations; its import target MUST NOT form part of the selector. Other items without a suitable name MUST have a kind and positional disambiguator. Selector spelling MUST be documented and reversible when names or types contain delimiter characters.
In `src/lib.rs`, `fn outer() { fn inner() {} }` gives the selectors `fn[outer]` and `fn[outer]/fn[inner]`. {cite}`requirements.references.rust_item_selectors`

In `src/lib.rs`, a method `run` in `impl Thing` has selector `impl[Thing]/fn[run]`; a method `run` in `impl Trait for Thing` has selector `impl[Thing/Trait]/fn[run]`; and a method `read` declared in `trait Read` has selector `trait[Read]/fn[read]`. {cite}`requirements.references.rust_item_selectors`

A function `run` inside an inline `mod local { ... }` in `src/lib.rs` has selector `mod[local]/fn[run]`. A function defined in a separate `src/local.rs` file has a selector within that file, without reconstructing the path of a `mod local;` declaration elsewhere. A foreign function `puts` in an `extern "C"` block has selector `extern[C]/fn[puts]`. {cite}`requirements.references.rust_item_selectors`

Two sibling declarations named `run` in one file, guarded by different `#[cfg]` attributes, have selectors `fn[run]#1` and `fn[run]#2` in source order. Their source line numbers are not part of either selector. {cite}`requirements.references.rust_item_selectors`

For consecutive sibling declarations `use alpha::A;` and `use beta::B;`, the selectors are `use#1` and `use#2`. Changing an import target leaves that declaration's positional selector the same and changes its raw evidence input. A named declaration such as `struct Packet;` instead has selector `struct[Packet]`. {cite}`requirements.references.rust_item_selectors` {cite}`requirements.ci.rust_item_inputs`

For a function preceded by a doc comment, an attribute, and an attached citation comment, a Rust-item input starts at the earliest attached line and ends at the function's final line. Its `text` contains those complete raw source lines. Inserting lines before them changes the displayed range without changing the input. {cite}`requirements.ci.rust_item_inputs`

For `impl Thing { fn run() {} }` on one line, `habeas add-input --for-requirement requirements.foo --rust-item src/lib.rs:1` adds separate inputs for `impl[Thing]` and `impl[Thing]/fn[run]`. Both contain the complete raw line. {cite}`requirements.cli.add_input_rust_item`

Given a requirement `foo.a.bar` and a named example `foo.a.b.bar`, `foo.*.bar` matches both, in that order. A requirements input stores both full names and their complete raw fenced declarations. Adding another matching definition invalidates the existing input. {cite}`requirements.references.definition_globs` {cite}`requirements.ci.requirements_inputs`
